readerTitle: Your rival wants to sell you his company. Four calls to make.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (지역 냉난방·배관 서비스 회사가 경쟁사를 인수, 경쟁사 매출 일부는 부동산 관리회사와의 B2B 유지보수 계약) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 경쟁사 인수는 '살까 말까' 한 번의 결정이 아니다. 왜 사는지, 무엇이 진짜 절감인지, 무엇을 빼야 하는지, 어떻게 합칠지라는 네 번의 결정이 이어진다.
misconception: 경쟁사를 사면 덩치가 커지고 경쟁자가 사라지니 그 자체로 이득이다. 매도자가 제시한 시너지 목록만큼 더 지불해도 된다.

sources.text: 기업 인수, 시너지 평가, 포트폴리오, 인수 후 통합에 관한 경영전략의 표준 개념 (STR-09 유닛 내용 종합)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 시너지 계산: 배차 사무실 통합 $90k + 이동 시간 절감 $80k = 비용 시너지 $170k, 여기에 교차판매 $130k를 더하면 매도자 주장 $300k. 카드 문구와 일치하는지 다시 확인하세요.
호가 $2.4M = 연간 이익 $400k × 6배. 경쟁사 매출의 40%가 부동산 관리회사 3곳과의 연 단위 계약이라는 설정도 카드 간에 일관되는지 확인하세요.
Watch out 카드의 경쟁 당국 관련 문장은 일반론으로만 썼습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Your biggest rival wants to sell you his company.
body: You run a heating and plumbing company with 20 technicians. For ten years, your toughest competitor has been Ray, who runs a 12-person shop across town.
Ray calls on a Monday. He's retiring. He'd rather sell to you than to a stranger. Over the next four cards, you make the calls.

image.label: Two service vans parked nose to nose on a quiet street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주택가 골목에 색이 다른 서비스 밴 두 대가 마주 보고 서 있고, 각 운전석에서 사장 두 명이 창문 너머로 악수. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What Ray is selling.
body: Ray's company earns about **$400,000** a year in profit. He's asking $2.4 million, six times that.

His vans cover many of the same neighborhoods as yours. About 40% of his revenue comes from yearly maintenance contracts with three property management firms. He also runs a small pool-cleaning side business.
He wants an answer within a month.

image.label: Map with two overlapping service areas
image.brief: 도시 지도 인포그래픽. 파란 원(우리 회사)과 주황 원(경쟁사)의 서비스 지역이 크게 겹치고, 겹친 부분을 진하게 표시. 한쪽 구석에 아파트 건물 아이콘 3개("3 property managers")와 작은 수영장 아이콘.

cards.title: Why would you buy?
body: Before talking price, you need one clear reason. Which one would you build the deal on?

options.text: If I don't, someone bigger will buy him and compete harder
options.feedback: A real worry, but fear alone can't tell you what to pay. Defensive buyers often overpay because any price feels better than losing.

options.text: Our routes overlap, so combined crews can fit more jobs into each van-day
options.feedback: This reason is specific and checkable. You can count drive time today and estimate it after. It also tells you which parts of Ray's business matter most.

options.text: We'd be the biggest firm in town
options.feedback: Size feels like strength, but it isn't a reason. Being bigger can add costs, like more managers and more scheduling chaos, without adding profit.

cards.title: Ray's broker sends a list of savings.
body: Say you chose route density. The broker says combining saves $300,000 a year: one shared dispatch office ($90k), less drive time ($80k), and selling your water-heater installs to Ray's customers ($130k).
How much of that do you count when you set your top price?

options.text: All $300k. The broker did the homework
options.feedback: You'd pay Ray in advance for sales that depend on customers choosing to buy more. If they don't, you've overpaid with no way back.

options.text: The $170k in cost savings you control. Treat cross-selling as a bonus
options.feedback: Cutting a dispatch office is in your hands. Getting customers to buy more is not. You stay competitive on price without betting on hopes.

options.text: None. Pay only what Ray's business is worth alone
options.feedback: The safest price, but another buyer who shares some real savings with Ray can easily outbid you.

cards.title: What about the pool business?
body: Say you priced on the $170k. Now look at Ray's pool-cleaning side business: two staff, busy only in summer, roughly breaking even. It shares nothing with your routes or skills.
What do you do with it?

options.text: Keep it and grow it. More services, more revenue
options.feedback: It pulls your attention to a business with different customers, seasons and skills. Your reason for buying was route density, and pools add none.

options.text: Leave it out of the deal, or let Ray sell it to a local pool company
options.feedback: You buy only what fits your reason for buying. A pool specialist will likely run it better and may pay Ray more for it than it's worth to you.

options.text: Keep it as is. It's too small to matter
options.feedback: Low risk in dollars. But small side businesses still take manager time, and that time comes out of the main job.

cards.title: The deal closes. Now what?
body: Say you bought the heating and plumbing business only. Ray's three property managers know Ray, not you. His best technicians are getting calls from other shops.
How do you combine the two companies?

options.text: Rebrand everything and move all staff to your pay and schedules in week one
options.feedback: Fast, but it changes everything for people at the moment they're most unsure. Top technicians leave, and a property manager may use the change as a reason to reopen bidding.

options.text: Merge dispatch and billing first, keep Ray's name for six months, have Ray introduce you to the property managers, and pay key techs to stay
options.feedback: You capture the dispatch and drive-time savings first, then protect the 40% of revenue tied to three relationships. The full change takes longer but loses less.

options.text: Run the two companies side by side for good, to avoid any disruption
options.feedback: Nobody quits, but there's no shared dispatch and no shorter routes. The $170k you paid for never arrives.

cards.title: Real deals are messier than four clean calls.
body: This story assumed Ray's numbers were true. In practice you check the books, the contracts and the staff turnover before you sign. Surprises found later cost far more.
Buying a direct competitor can also draw a regulator's attention in some markets. Get local advice before you commit.
cards.softwareNote: The same four calls apply when a software company buys a rival tool. Shared hosting and support are savings you control. Moving the rival's users onto your product is the integration step where churn usually spikes.

cards.title: Buying a competitor is four decisions, not one.
body: Each call you made maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Why buy:** a specific, checkable reason, like route density (Why companies acquire)
**What to pay for:** only the savings you control (Real vs imagined synergies)
**What to drop:** parts that don't fit your reason (Portfolio thinking and spin-offs)
**How to combine:** quick back-office wins first, people and customers protected (Integration)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** name one company you could imagine buying. Write your one reason in a single sentence. If you can't, you're not ready to talk price.
